item.title: Nearly 25 Years Later, Metal Gear Solid 2's First Boss Skip Makes Modern Stealth Games Look Too Scripted
item.description:
A new speedrunning exploit has been discovered in Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty , one that allows players to skip the game's first boss fight with Olga Gurlukovich during the Tanker mission. This discovery marks the first-ever recorded boss skip in Metal Gear Solid 2 , and makes for a fairly significant shake-up for the speedrunning scene.

Metal Gear Solid 2 , unlike subsequent games, relies on quasi-metroidvania elements for progression through its two campaign "maps." The player is introduced to this concept in the opening Tanker mission, which is famously the only part of Metal Gear Solid 2 that sees you playing as Solid Snake himself. As is his MO, Solid begins this mission with minimal gear, not even bothering to bring any weapons beyond an M9 tranquilizer pistol. Unfortunately, he needs a real gun to disable explosives barring his path to Metal Gear Ray, and the only way to obtain an appropriate gun is to defeat Olga, another infiltrator. This showdown serves as Olga's introduction as well as an extended combat tutorial, and is quite time-consuming. But, as proven by speedrunner apel on YouTube, it apparently can be avoided altogether.

Every Metal Gear Solid Game In Chronological Order (And The Year They Take Place In)

The Metal Gear Solid games span across decades, though not in chronological order. This should clear the timeline up.

By David Heath

How Metal Gear Solid 2's Newly Discovered Olga Skip Highlights Its Enduring Strengths

To achieve the Olga skip, you have to drag an unconscious guard to an explosives-laden hallway blocking the way to the hold, where Colonel Dolph is making a speech and presenting Metal Gear Ray. Normally, the only way to disable these explosives would be to shoot the consoles powering the motion-sensing lasers, which can only work with Olga's pistol. But if you place the knocked-out guard beneath the lasers, he'll activate the explosives when he wakes up. This will generally result in a game over, but by timing Snake's positioning just right, you can essentially make the game "flag" that the explosives have already been detonated, thus allowing you to progress after reloading the game.

The benefits that this discovery will have for the Metal Gear Solid speedrunning community are obvious. Even for experienced players, Olga often serves as a major slowdown point in the Tanker chapter, as Snake's M9 isn't exactly the most effective weapon, and Olga's use of cover means that unloading a clip for a quick victory isn't really feasible. With this newly discovered exploit, you can get past the explosives-rigged hallway and be well on your way to Metal Gear Ray mere minutes after starting the game.

It doesn't appear that this Olga boss skip actually impacts the Metal Gear Solid 2 story at all. The rest of the game unfolds as though Snake and Olga had already met regardless.

Players Are Still Discovering New Secrets in Metal Gear Solid 2

Aside from being a win for speedrunners, this new MGS2 discovery helps underscore what makes Metal Gear such a great franchise. Metal Gear Solid 2 , in particular, has aged incredibly well, and even first-time players today will remark upon how "good," simply put, it feels to play. A lot of this can be attributed to its numerous interweaving systems, which still lead to surprises more than two decades later. For instance, shortly before this Olga skip was discovered, MGS2 players learned that Raiden can reduce his visibility throughout the Plant mission by wearing the BDU disguise.

In a contemporary stealth game (let's say, Assassin's Creed or Ghost of Yotei ), I never expect to be surprised by mechanics or systems. I may be surprised by certain plot beats or even missions/setpieces, but at the end of the day, I know that the gameplay is going to boil down to pressing the "kill" button at the proper moment, hiding behind walls, and maybe using a straightforward tool like a smoke bomb to get out of a jam. These games, despite having the benefit of hindsight and new tech, lack the collaborative complexity of a Metal Gear Solid 2 .

Systems Depth Is What Keeps Metal Gear Solid 2 Timeless

I only recently replayed Metal Gear Solid 2 , so the nuances of its gameplay are especially fresh in my mind. I didn't leverage the aforementioned Olga-skip exploit in my last run, but I did make several personal discoveries about the game, even though I've beaten it multiple times.

Aside from being a win for speedrunners, this new MGS2 discovery helps underscore what makes Metal Gear such a great franchise.

One that stands out occurred during the Emma Emmerich escort mission. Emma is deathly afraid of bugs, and there's a swarm of roaches blocking the path forward at one point. When I first played MGS2 , I looked up the "proper" way to solve this problem: by spraying the coolant tool to disperse the bugs. But on my second playthrough, I realized that I could simply grapple Emma and drag her to the elevator. On my third and most recent playthrough, I discovered that you can actually knock Emma out entirely, and simply drag her to the elevator that way. Not the most ethical methods, but they get the job done.

Nearly 25 Years Later, Metal Gear Solid 2's First Boss Skip Makes Modern Stealth Games Look Too Scripted
New Official Metal Gear Solid Release Confirmed for November
6 PlayStation 2 Classics That Hold Up As 10/10 Masterpieces
What is the Future of Metal Gear Solid?

I first played Metal Gear Solid 2 when I was a young teenager, but already I had been conditioned by contemporary gaming to expect one, proper way of accomplishing a goal. Freedom for me, at that time, boiled down to whether I wanted to attack a fortress from the left or the right in games like Far Cry 3 . What I realized later, as my tastes changed and evolved, is that the Metal Gear games are deeply reactive as a rule, anticipating the player's moves and teeing up unique reactions for them. This complex web of different systems is what allows for things like the Olga skip, and I'm left wishing we still got AAA games as sophisticated as this 2001 title.

item.title: Final Fantasy 13's Lightning Finally Returning on October 22
item.description:
Final Fantasy has never been particularly shy about revisiting its own history, which is why one of the best Final Fantasy protagonists, Lightning, is relevant in October 2026. Characters, worlds, and ideas from across the franchise have repeatedly found their way into new games, even when their original stories were finished years earlier. It's always creative, too, to see how a game justifies bringing together different heroes into a single roster when they otherwise have little reason to share the same world.

Said approach allows newer Final Fantasy games to reach far beyond their own stories. A character from one numbered entry can suddenly appear alongside heroes from another, creating combinations that would never happen in a traditional Final Fantasy sequel. Sure, having a solo hero return is cool, but seeing the various Final Fantasy protagonists stand together is another story.

Final Fantasy 10: Eternal Calm Officially Confirmed for November 2026

As a continued celebration of its 25th anniversary, Final Fantasy 10 fans have a new release coming in November 2026.

3
By Joshua Duckworth

Final Fantasy 13's Lightning Still Resonates with Fans

Lightning is coming back in Final Fantasy Resonance , which is set to release on October 22, but she isn't the only Final Fantasy character appearing in the upcoming HD-2D RPG, joining a crossover cast that spans much of the franchise's history. Her inclusion gives Final Fantasy 13 representation in a game specifically designed to bring together characters from different eras of the series.

Final Fantasy Resonance is not a traditional remake or sequel, either. The game takes place in the Kingdom of Grandshelt and follows Rain, Lasswell, and Fina as they attempt to protect the kingdom's remaining crystals from Veritas of the Dark. Its turn-based combat is built around a new story and a Vision system that allows characters from previous Final Fantasy games to enter the adventure, with Lightning appearing alongside characters like Cloud, Tidus, Squall, Terra, Zidane, Noctis, and even Final Fantasy 16 's Clive.

Lightning has already been shown fighting in Final Fantasy Resonance , including alongside her Eidolon Odin. Other crossover characters have their own roles within the game, while Sephiroth is set to appear through a special challenge. The result is a roster that reaches from the earliest parts of Final Fantasy 's history to some of its newest entries, with the HD-2D presentation giving the entire project a distinctly different look from the numbered games these characters originally came from.

Final Fantasy Game is Permanently Shutting Down on October 6

Final Fantasy 14's Beastmaster Just Proved Pokemon's Best Idea Belongs in More RPGs

Players also don't have to wait until October 22 to see how Final Fantasy Resonance handles its unusual combination of original characters and franchise favorites. A free demo is currently available on PC, PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch, and Xbox Series X, covering the opening portion of the game and its first chapter (roughly three to five hours). Progress carries over to the full release, giving players a way to get started before Lightning and the rest of the crossover cast officially arrive later this month.

item.title: Hollow Knight: Silksong Fans Should Play Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Right Now, Because They Can
item.description:
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is slated to release on October 15, and fans of the franchise are beyond excited. While we wait for Castlevania: Belmont's Curse to cook up, Konami has shared a playable demo, keeping fans nice and occupied before the full game is available. This free-to-play demo, which spans about 30–45 minutes, is available now on the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch, and on Steam.

While playing through this new demo, I was reminded of another fan-favorite Metroidvania-style title, Hollow Knight: Silksong . While Castlevania and Hollow Knight have very distinct identities and quirks that make them special, gameplay, narrative tropes, and combat in both games are pretty similar. This demo offered me a taste of both titles that I love so much, and reminded me why the world of demos can be a tricky place if not handled with care.

A New Main Series Castlevania Game Was Just Revealed, But Its Art Style Might Be Controversial

Konami announces its first original, mainline Castlevania title in more than ten years during Sony's hour-long State of Play.

By Kendall Cunningham

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse and Hollow Knight: Silksong are Almost One and the Same

Check Out the Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Demo on Steam

Castlevania is a heavy-hitter, holding it down as one of the most famous side-scrollers out there. Fans of the franchise will note the latest entry, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, is yet another 2D side-scroller, a format that Konami has seemingly mastered. The free-to-play demo allows players a look at the opening sequence of the game, where they can test out mechanics and get to know the main protagonist, Rose Belmont. Set in monster-ridden Paris in 1499, Rose and her father, Trevor, are called on to dispatch these demonic creatures from the city's streets. In such little time, players are already immersed in this new world, caught up in what Rose and her father must do to survive.

While her father investigates, Rose heads out on her lonesome, armed with enchanted tarot cards and her Arcane Whip to snuff out the source of the evil. While I haven't gotten to know her for that long just yet, piloting Rose has already gotten me hooked on the character. She's strong and duty-bound, determined to flush out evil at any cost. Rose already comes off as a lethal warrior, a real badass in her own right. Expert voice acting from Abby Trott only aids in Rose's characterization, making her seem untouchable.

Upon traversing the first level, players will be treated to illustrated cutscenes that offer a reprieve from the combat, which beautifully highlight characters and their layouts.

Music swells as players forge on, orchestral and gothic, a moody setting for a moody game. Movement is fast-paced and fluid, while combat relies on snappy and satisfying combos a la your whip, aka the Vampire Killer. It seems like Rose' whip also acts as a traversal tool, utilized to grapple both enemies and swing from anchor points. This detail should open up exploration even further, allowing players to traverse areas as they please, whether on foot or by swinging from anchor to anchor.

The action-packed demo ends in a boss fight in a grotesque sewer-like setting where players must take on The Fallen. Players must use claws, holy cross attacks, and wide-reaching maneuvers to down this baddie. After taking The Fallen out, players will unlock the "Blood Tells" achievement. It is worth noting that any progress and save data made via the demo does carry over directly to the full version of the game once it launches, so people won't have to go through the hassle of starting all over again.

I implore people to try their hand at the demo. It is a full-fleshed-out work that gets people invested in the new title ahead of the release. Upon picking up the demo, folks will notice a couple of things, especially those who might be fans of a little title called Hollow Knight: Silksong . Both have that instantly recognizable Metroidvania DNA, which focuses on maze-like 2D settings where progress is made by acquiring new abilities or items found throughout. Both titles feature fast-paced combat with demanding fights that push players to the limit each time.

Fluid combat is a crux of both titles, a style that almost feels like dancing. Mobility for characters is acrobatic, focusing on diagonal aerial strikes and snappy dashes. Key weapons, like Rose's whip or Hornet's blade, called The Needle, are utilized in 2D constraints, featuring fixed arcs, save for a few vertical moves Rose can pull off. These directional attacks are powerful and clean, letting players take out enemies quickly before readjusting with a back step or dash. While it is too early to say, it seems like Castlevania: Belmont's Curse will also have a backtracking element in order to reach previously closed-off areas. Backtracking is also key to the story of Hollow Knight: Silksong and is featured heavily when players take on side-quests or if they want to check out settlements discovered early on.

This is yet another aspect that makes both titles Metroidvania-esque. As mentioned, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse will seemingly feature a grapple mechanic, allowing Rose to get around stages or enemies. Hornet's needle and thread essentially do the same thing . From combat fluidity to narrative structure with backtracking as a central theme, both games share immense similarities. If fans of Hollow Knight: Silksong are looking to scratch that Metroidvania itch but don't know where to look, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a great jumping-off point. Once released, the Castlevania playthrough should stave off any hankering for a third Hollow Knight title, at least for a while.

A Proper Demo Is Sometimes Almost Better Than the Full Game

Demos are meant to hook audiences in, sharing a look at gameplay, narrative, and characters before a full release. Castlevania: Belmont's Curse' s demo does just that, successfully hooking players in and setting them up for the full game to come in mid-October. There have been times when demos end up being the more memorable portion of the release process, sharing a snippet of the game that becomes its best parts. This is largely due to demos containing misleading gameplay or settings that end up being somewhat scrapped in the final game. There is no worse feeling than booting up a game you've been waiting for, only for it not to live up to the hype conjured up via the demo.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a classic example of a demo with ever-so-slightly misleading content. The standalone teaser demo titled "Beginning Hour" serves as a sort of separate story from the main game with interwoven similarities here and there. Players are captives in the Baker house deep down in the bayou, seemingly all alone in the dark. They must piece together clues while traversing this dilapidated house, solving puzzles and defending themselves against grotesque monsters. The teaser is beyond spooky, with an eerie, claustrophobic feel. While I think the full game encapsulates this feeling, it really only does so within the first house section, rather than carrying that same vibe throughout its entirety. I still think that the full game is impeccable, but the demo's tone is slightly misleading in my opinion. I wasn't disappointed in any way, just a little confused.

I implore people to try their hand at the demo. It is a full-fleshed-out work that gets people invested in the new title ahead of the release.

​​​​​​​Rather than being misleading, some game demos can also turn out better than the full release, which is very disappointing for some. Metal Gear Solid 2 's demo is iconic. Titled "The Tanker," this demo was bundled with Zone of the Enders, which was meant to generate hype, and boy, were people hyped. The demo offered a sneak peek at one of the most anticipated video game sequels, and it didn't disappoint. Action-packed and stealthy, the gameplay featured first-person aiming, peeking, and shooting from cover, all new additions to the franchise at the time.

CD Projekt Red Just Got The Witcher 3's Best Quest Writer Back, and Ciri Has the Most to Gain
Fallout 76's New Roadmap Is Quietly Turning the Online RPG Into Fallout 5's Most Important Test Run
Nearly 25 Years Later, Metal Gear Solid 2's First Boss Skip Makes Modern Stealth Games Look Too Scripted
Hollow Knight: Silksong Fans Should Play Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Right Now, Because They Can

Legendary spy and top-notch soldier Solid Snake is tasked with infiltrating a military ship on the Hudson River. The best part of that demo, as silly as it sounds, is the rain effect. This detail, at the time, was pretty jaw-dropping, affecting the way the player sees while in first-person. In short, good demos can be the key to a full game's success, but they can also be their downfall. Companies need to strike a balance, sharing gameplay with audiences that keeps them interested while ensuring that gameplay is consistent with what is presented in the full game.

While Castlevania and Hollow Knight have very distinct identities and quirks that make them special, gameplay, narrative tropes, and combat in both games are pretty similar. This demo offered me a taste of both titles that I love so much, and reminded me why the world of demos can be a tricky place if not handled with care.

A New Main Series Castlevania Game Was Just Revealed, But Its Art Style Might Be Controversial

Konami announces its first original, mainline Castlevania title in more than ten years during Sony's hour-long State of Play.

By Kendall Cunningham

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse and Hollow Knight: Silksong are Almost One and the Same

Check Out the Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Demo on Steam

Castlevania is a heavy-hitter, holding it down as one of the most famous side-scrollers out there. Fans of the franchise will note the latest entry, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, is yet another 2D side-scroller, a format that Konami has seemingly mastered. The free-to-play demo allows players a look at the opening sequence of the game, where they can test out mechanics and get to know the main protagonist, Rose Belmont. Set in monster-ridden Paris in 1499, Rose and her father, Trevor, are called on to dispatch these demonic creatures from the city's streets. In such little time, players are already immersed in this new world, caught up in what Rose and her father must do to survive.

While her father investigates, Rose heads out on her lonesome, armed with enchanted tarot cards and her Arcane Whip to snuff out the source of the evil. While I haven't gotten to know her for that long just yet, piloting Rose has already gotten me hooked on the character. She's strong and duty-bound, determined to flush out evil at any cost. Rose already comes off as a lethal warrior, a real badass in her own right. Expert voice acting from Abby Trott only aids in Rose's characterization, making her seem untouchable.

Upon traversing the first level, players will be treated to illustrated cutscenes that offer a reprieve from the combat, which beautifully highlight characters and their layouts.

Music swells as players forge on, orchestral and gothic, a moody setting for a moody game. Movement is fast-paced and fluid, while combat relies on snappy and satisfying combos a la your whip, aka the Vampire Killer. It seems like Rose' whip also acts as a traversal tool, utilized to grapple both enemies and swing from anchor points. This detail should open up exploration even further, allowing players to traverse areas as they please, whether on foot or by swinging from anchor to anchor.

The action-packed demo ends in a boss fight in a grotesque sewer-like setting where players must take on The Fallen. Players must use claws, holy cross attacks, and wide-reaching maneuvers to down this baddie. After taking The Fallen out, players will unlock the "Blood Tells" achievement. It is worth noting that any progress and save data made via the demo does carry over directly to the full version of the game once it launches, so people won't have to go through the hassle of starting all over again.

I implore people to try their hand at the demo. It is a full-fleshed-out work that gets people invested in the new title ahead of the release. Upon picking up the demo, folks will notice a couple of things, especially those who might be fans of a little title called Hollow Knight: Silksong . Both have that instantly recognizable Metroidvania DNA, which focuses on maze-like 2D settings where progress is made by acquiring new abilities or items found throughout. Both titles feature fast-paced combat with demanding fights that push players to the limit each time.

Fluid combat is a crux of both titles, a style that almost feels like dancing. Mobility for characters is acrobatic, focusing on diagonal aerial strikes and snappy dashes. Key weapons, like Rose's whip or Hornet's blade, called The Needle, are utilized in 2D constraints, featuring fixed arcs, save for a few vertical moves Rose can pull off. These directional attacks are powerful and clean, letting players take out enemies quickly before readjusting with a back step or dash. While it is too early to say, it seems like Castlevania: Belmont's Curse will also have a backtracking element in order to reach previously closed-off areas. Backtracking is also key to the story of Hollow Knight: Silksong and is featured heavily when players take on side-quests or if they want to check out settlements discovered early on.

This is yet another aspect that makes both titles Metroidvania-esque. As mentioned, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse will seemingly feature a grapple mechanic, allowing Rose to get around stages or enemies. Hornet's needle and thread essentially do the same thing . From combat fluidity to narrative structure with backtracking as a central theme, both games share immense similarities. If fans of Hollow Knight: Silksong are looking to scratch that Metroidvania itch but don't know where to look, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a great jumping-off point. Once released, the Castlevania playthrough should stave off any hankering for a third Hollow Knight title, at least for a while.

A Proper Demo Is Sometimes Almost Better Than the Full Game

Demos are meant to hook audiences in, sharing a look at gameplay, narrative, and characters before a full release. Castlevania: Belmont's Curse' s demo does just that, successfully hooking players in and setting them up for the full game to come in mid-October. There have been times when demos end up being the more memorable portion of the release process, sharing a snippet of the game that becomes its best parts. This is largely due to demos containing misleading gameplay or settings that end up being somewhat scrapped in the final game. There is no worse feeling than booting up a game you've been waiting for, only for it not to live up to the hype conjured up via the demo.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a classic example of a demo with ever-so-slightly misleading content. The standalone teaser demo titled "Beginning Hour" serves as a sort of separate story from the main game with interwoven similarities here and there. Players are captives in the Baker house deep down in the bayou, seemingly all alone in the dark. They must piece together clues while traversing this dilapidated house, solving puzzles and defending themselves against grotesque monsters. The teaser is beyond spooky, with an eerie, claustrophobic feel. While I think the full game encapsulates this feeling, it really only does so within the first house section, rather than carrying that same vibe throughout its entirety. I still think that the full game is impeccable, but the demo's tone is slightly misleading in my opinion. I wasn't disappointed in any way, just a little confused.

I implore people to try their hand at the demo. It is a full-fleshed-out work that gets people invested in the new title ahead of the release.

​​​​​​​Rather than being misleading, some game demos can also turn out better than the full release, which is very disappointing for some. Metal Gear Solid 2 's demo is iconic. Titled "The Tanker," this demo was bundled with Zone of the Enders, which was meant to generate hype, and boy, were people hyped. The demo offered a sneak peek at one of the most anticipated video game sequels, and it didn't disappoint. Action-packed and stealthy, the gameplay featured first-person aiming, peeking, and shooting from cover, all new additions to the franchise at the time.

CD Projekt Red Just Got The Witcher 3's Best Quest Writer Back, and Ciri Has the Most to Gain
Fallout 76's New Roadmap Is Quietly Turning the Online RPG Into Fallout 5's Most Important Test Run
Nearly 25 Years Later, Metal Gear Solid 2's First Boss Skip Makes Modern Stealth Games Look Too Scripted
Hollow Knight: Silksong Fans Should Play Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Right Now, Because They Can

Legendary spy and top-notch soldier Solid Snake is tasked with infiltrating a military ship on the Hudson River. The best part of that demo, as silly as it sounds, is the rain effect. This detail, at the time, was pretty jaw-dropping, affecting the way the player sees while in first-person. In short, good demos can be the key to a full game's success, but they can also be their downfall. Companies need to strike a balance, sharing gameplay with audiences that keeps them interested while ensuring that gameplay is consistent with what is presented in the full game.

item.title: Skate 3 in Call of Duty Is Wild, but AI Is Tackling a Much Bigger Gaming Problem
item.description:
AI is probably the most talked-about topic in the entire world right now, and in gaming, the technology is becoming increasingly intertwined with just about every aspect of the industry. Whether it's used for designing the next Call of Duty , coding NPCs in Fallout , or ideas for a new soulslike, AI is here to stay, and one of the more interesting spaces that has recently evolved rapidly is modding. Video game mods have been around for decades, with some games being completely transformed by a couple of quick installs, but things are about to get a whole lot more interesting thanks to these newer, highly advanced AI models.

Anthropic just released Opus 5.5 into the wild, and within a few short days, we have seen some of the strangest Frankenstein creations the gaming world has ever seen. Anything from Call of Duty guns in Minecraft to Skate 3 being usable on iconic maps like Rust, it feels like Pandora's box has been opened and the modding side of gaming has been delivered an astronomical curveball. Additionally, this same technology is already being applied to decompilation ports and additional means of emulation, allowing more older games to be preserved on modern hardware and playable for the first time on PC.

6 Best Games That Started As Half-Life Mods, Ranked

These games had humble beginnings first as mere Half-Life mods, but have since grown into massive phenomena.

By Morgan P

Skating Around in Call Of Duty Is Just the Beginning

AI's implementation in gaming has ramped up exponentially in a few short years. A while ago, the term simply referred to enemy behavior or world generation, but now, we are seeing AI applied in more places than ever before. One of the most prominent use cases is in upscaling, with DLSS 5 showing off an uncanny level of detail that will no doubt only get scarier in the coming months. Then there have been a handful of AI assets showing up in big-budget games, yet I think the biggest leap in the industry's relationship with the technology has just been seen in the form of modding.

In the past, video game mods were only made possible by talented coders and artists who were willing to take the time to build an entirely new set of rules on top of an existing product. Depending on the game and the developer's support for these projects, you could have just a handful of mods or literally thousands, ranging from QoL tweaks to extensive overhauls. Now, though, by using AI to rewrite the code of a game, you are able to rapidly merge logic and mechanics from other games, borrowing and swapping parts to create an amalgamation of completely different things.

Some of the AI-Powered Gaming Mashups Making the Rounds

  • Minecraft+Skate3+Call of Duty
  • Portal+Call of Duty Zombies
  • Mario+Halo

From a technical perspective, these aren't mods in the traditional sense. The people prompting the agents are not just merging several games into one and calling it a day; instead, they are asking the AI to rewrite the existing code from these games and iterating the result until it reaches the state seen in the viral clips. That means that while it may look like an effortless creation that was made through typing a single command, in order to achieve these crazy modded states, it may actually take days, weeks, or even months to reach that level, though things will only improve from here.

And, like anything related to AI, these projects are being received with a fair share of criticism. Firstly, to a lot of people, the mash-up games feel fairly soulless and more like a random set of mechanics merged together for a launch, rather than presenting something of actual substance. For me, though, the more curious discussion comes from how much the technology is playing with the original creator's vision. Game devs have always had different stances on mods and whether they are okay with them, but this appears like a much bolder step that may be taking things a tad too far in terms of breaking down the initial creative visions of so many talented people.

Ports And Emulators For Everything

On the other side of the fence of these aggressive modded games is emulation and decompilation. Much to the dismay of millions of players, not every game is available on PC, and that's why a lot of players turn to emulation and unofficial ports to allow them to replay, or experience for the first time, so many classic games across several generations of consoles. As people have gotten better at understanding how certain platforms function, we have seen far more games become available, to the point where we are frequently seeing current generation exclusives appear on PC every other week.

That's where the AI comes in, as for decompilation projects that aim to port and preserve otherwise inaccessible games, fans are now able to leverage the technology to achieve that goal even faster. Before, decompiling meant writing code to effectively reverse-engineer the ones and zeros into something usable, which, as it turns out, is a perfect test for AI. What that means in practice is more platform-locked games are being unlocked and are now playable in a much better form than traditional emulation, giving even the most obscure titles a second lease on life.

As great as all that sounds, it still comes with some major caveats. Major game companies like Nintendo and PlayStation have already made it very clear that they would rather keep their games to themselves, and have been continuing to crack down on modding software and emulators, but as fast as they are to shut things down, the project developers seem to be even faster. Enormous strides have been taken in projects like KytyPS5, where we are now seeing Marvel's Wolverine booting on PC, less than a month after launch, yet as good as these programs get, I have no doubt that they will remain just out of reach for your average person to come along and play with a single click.

CD Projekt Red Just Got The Witcher 3's Best Quest Writer Back, and Ciri Has the Most to Gain
Fallout 76's New Roadmap Is Quietly Turning the Online RPG Into Fallout 5's Most Important Test Run
Hollow Knight: Silksong Fans Should Play Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Right Now, Because They Can
5 Single-Player FPS Games Perfect For Blowing Off Steam

And for the other mashup projects, they still require existing copies to extract the files from the first place, so we are still a long way off from seeing fully AI-generated games appear in the blink of an eye. At the same time, it is hard to deny just how impressive all of these mods, ports, emulators, and decompilations are, and I imagine we will find a middle ground between instantaneous creation and genuinely helpful tools that improve everyone's gaming experience, from the developer all the way to the players at the end of the line.

item.title: What is Enemy Upscaling in The Witcher 3?
item.description:
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered version of the game has a feature called Enemy Upscaling as one of the toggleable options in gameplay settings. However, the game does not explain what this setting does, leaving players who are unfamiliar with the terminology confused about whether or not they should turn it on. Here’s how it works.

The Witcher 3: Most Useful Skills And Abilities

The Witcher 3 has tons of different skills players can take advantage of. These skills and abilities are so good any Witcher would want to have them.

By Ritwik Mitra

What is Enemy Upscaling in The Witcher 3?

Enemy Upscaling is a feature that automatically increases the level of lower-level enemies to match Geralt’s current level at every point in the game.

For instance, a Drowner in White Orchard is typically around level 3-5.

  • If Enemy Upscaling is turned off , this Drowner will remain at level 3-5 no matter what level Geralt reaches in the game. So a level 1 Geralt will face a level 3 Drowner in White Orchard, and a level 50 Geralt will also face a level 3 Drowner in the same location.
  • If Enemy Upscaling is turned on , the Drowner’s level will increase alongside Geralt’s level. So a level 1 Geralt will find a level 3 Drowner in White Orchard, but a level 50 Geralt will find a level 48-50 Drowner in the same location, its level artificially boosted to match yours.

Enemy Upscaling only scales in one direction: upwards. Weaker enemies are made stronger, but stronger enemies aren’t forcefully weakened.

How to Turn On Enemy Upscaling

Go to Settings → Gameplay → Enemy Upscaling and toggle the setting ON or OFF.

Should You Turn Enemy Upscaling On or Off in The Witcher 3?

Whether or not you should use Enemy Upscaling is a matter of personal preference . The great thing is that this option is freely toggleable, which means if you don’t like it for any reason or want to try it out for a bit just to see, you can turn it on and off at any time, and the changes will take effect instantly.

To give you a clearer perspective, here are the pros and cons of Enemy Upscaling in The Witcher 3 :

Pros

  • Geralt never becomes overpowered enough to make a combat encounter trivial. Great for players who get bored when they don’t feel challenged.
  • You get more incentive to use potions, decoctions, oils, bombs, and other tools in Geralt’s kit.
  • Prevents early game quests from becoming a complete cakewalk if you tackle them later on.

Cons

  • Since everyone levels with you, there is a lack of a sense of progression. Gear upgrades and new skills merely feel like you’re keeping pace, not getting stronger.
  • Swarming enemies like rats, dogs, and wolves become a huge problem at higher levels.
